title: ref locals, ref structs, scoped and unsafe code
body: `ref` can do more than pass parameters. A `ref` local aliases another variable (`ref int slot = ref array[2];`), and a method can return by reference (`ref int Find(...)`) so callers update storage in place, avoiding copies of large structs. `ref readonly` returns allow aliasing without mutation. A struct method cannot return a reference to its own fields (CS8170) because `this` may be a temporary copy; classes can, since their fields live in the heap object.

`ref struct` types (like `Span<T>`) may live only on the stack. Since C# 11 a ref struct can hold `ref` fields, which is how `Span<T>` itself is written. The compiler tracks 'escape scope' to stop a reference to a local from leaking out of the method. The `scoped` modifier promises a parameter or local will not escape, which lets the compiler accept more code safely.

Unsafe code (`unsafe` blocks, enabled with `AllowUnsafeBlocks`) uses raw pointers: `int*`, `&x`, `*p`, pointer arithmetic, `stackalloc` to a pointer, `sizeof`, and `fixed` to pin a managed object so the GC cannot move it while you hold its address. Function pointers (`delegate*<int, int>`) call methods without delegate allocation, mainly for interop.

Unsafe code disables the safety guarantees: an out-of-bounds pointer write silently corrupts memory. Most performance needs are met with spans and `ref` locals instead. Interop with native libraries uses `[LibraryImport]` (source-generated marshalling) rather than hand-written pointers where possible.

C# 15 begins redefining unsafe so that only memory-accessing operations require `unsafe` (final stage). Today, check every `unsafe` block for bounds, pinning duration and aliasing, and keep it as small as possible.
challenge: Write a method ref int FirstNegative(Span<int> values) that returns a reference to the first negative element (throw if none) and use it to set that element to 0 in [5, -2, -7].
question: What does the `fixed` statement do in unsafe code?
correct: Pins a managed object so the GC cannot move it while its address is used
wrong: Allocates memory outside the GC heap
reasoning: The GC compacts the heap; pinning keeps addresses valid for the duration of the fixed block only.
